SDK 1.0.0 · Bridge protocol v1
GitHub · Issues

Reference

Configuration

One object configures an embedded portal session on every platform: PortalSdkConfig in JavaScript, PortalConfig in Swift and Kotlin. It says where the portal lives, how it should present itself, and which development hatches are open.

Two rules are worth reading before the tables. Your baseUrl must include the portal's deploy path prefix — omitting it is the single most common integration failure. And the SDK does not theme the portal: a form's own colours and branding come from the tenant's branch, server-side. What you configure here is the SDK's own screens, plus the three appearance values the portal accepts.

The config object, per platform

Field names are deliberately the same across the four hosts, with two casing differences and two fields that exist on some platforms only. Those exceptions are listed in the option matrix; start from these four shapes.

  • React Native
  • Expo sheet
  • iOS
  • Android

React Native @amthal-group/portal-react-native

import { AmthalPortalForm } from '@amthal-group/portal-react-native';

<AmthalPortalForm
  config={{
    baseUrl: 'https://portal.example.com/portal',
    locale: 'en',
    theme: 'system',
    fontScale: 1.0,
    brandColor: '#121E4C',
    minPortalVersion: '1.8.0',
  }}
  request={{ kind: 'newApplication', type: 'internal', productID: 3021 }}
  auth={{ token, branchId: '12' }}
  onSubmitted={handleSubmitted}
  onCancelled={handleCancelled}
  onError={handleError}
  onCloseRequested={handleClose}
/>

Expo native sheet @amthal-group/portal-expo iOS only

import { presentPortalSheet } from '@amthal-group/portal-expo';

const session = presentPortalSheet({
  config: {
    baseUrl: 'https://portal.example.com/portal',
    locale: 'ar',
    theme: 'system',
    fontScale: 1.0,
  },
  auth: { token, branchId: '12' },
  request: { kind: 'newApplication', type: 'internal', productID: 3021 },
  sheet: { detents: ['large'], grabber: true },
  onSubmitted: (result) => console.log(result.applicationNo),
});

iOS (Swift) AmthalPortal

import AmthalPortal

let config = try PortalConfig(
    baseURL: URL(string: "https://portal.example.com/portal")!,
    locale: .en,
    theme: .system,
    fontScale: 1.0,
    brandColor: UIColor(red: 0.07, green: 0.12, blue: 0.30, alpha: 1),
    minPortalVersion: "1.8.0"
)

PortalConfig.init is throws on iOS — the two errors it can throw are listed under baseUrl.

Android (Kotlin) com.amthalgroup:portal-sdk

import com.amthalgroup.portal.PortalConfig
import com.amthalgroup.portal.PortalLocale
import com.amthalgroup.portal.PortalTheme

val config = PortalConfig(
    baseUrl = "https://portal.example.com/portal",
    locale = PortalLocale.EN,
    theme = PortalTheme.SYSTEM,
    fontScale = 1f,
    brandColor = Color.parseColor("#121E4C"),
    minPortalVersion = "1.8.0",
)

Option matrix

Which option exists where, and under which name. Everything except baseUrl is optional on every platform.

Availability and naming across the four hosts
Option React Native Expo sheet iOS Android
baseUrlbaseUrlbaseUrlbaseURL (a URL)baseUrl
localeYesYesYes PortalLocaleYes PortalLocale
themeYesYesYes PortalThemeYes PortalTheme
fontScaleYesYesYes DoubleYes Float
brandColorYes hex stringNoYes UIColor?Yes @ColorInt Int?
minPortalVersionYesYesYesYes
allowedOriginsYes string[]Yes string[]Yes Set<String>?Yes Set<String>
enableLoggingYesYesYesYes
Insecure-HTTP hatchallowInsecureHttpallowInsecureHttpallowInsecureHTTPallowInsecureHttp
certificatePinnerNoNoNoOnly here
Two casing traps

The insecure-HTTP flag is allowInsecureHTTP on iOS and allowInsecureHttp everywhere else. On the auth object, the optional user payload is user in JavaScript, userJSON in Swift and userJson in Kotlin. Neither split is a typo you can fix by guessing — copy the spelling for the platform you are on.

The Expo sheet has no brandColor

The field is absent from the Expo config type and the native module never reads one, so the sheet's loading interstitial always uses the platform default tint. If branding the wait matters to you, use the inline React Native component, which does support it.

baseUrl — required, and it must carry the deploy path

TypeReact Native, Expo, Android: string. iOS: URL.
DefaultNone — required.
Acceptshttps:// always; http:// for loopback hosts, or via the dev-only hatch.
RejectsCredentials in the URL and a query string. Android also rejects a fragment, at construction time.

The Client Portal is deployed under a base href of /portal/, so a correct value almost always ends in that prefix: 

https://portal.example.com/portal       correct
https://portal.example.com/portal/      correct — a trailing slash is tolerated
https://portal.example.com              WRONG — the deploy path is missing
https://portal.example.com/portal?x=1   WRONG — never a query string
Why the prefix is not optional

The SDK computes the navigation boundary as basePath + "/embed", where basePath is the path component of your baseUrl. Drop the /portal and every real portal URL looks like it sits outside the allowed subtree, so the portal's very first in-app navigation is treated as an external link. The symptom is not an error dialog — it is the user being thrown out of your app into Safari or Chrome on the first tap.

The one check that settles it, before you write any code. This must return JSON, not HTML:

curl -sI https://portal.example.com/portal/embed/manifest.json

content-type: application/json   correct
content-type: text/html          wrong — the SPA catch-all answered, so the path is wrong

A text/html answer means the manifest fetch will fail and the session ends in manifestFailed. The manifest is always read from the full base URL plus /embed/manifest.json — never from the bare origin, which is exactly why the prefix has to be in the value you configure.

What an invalid base URL does, per platform

PlatformBehaviour
React Native Nothing throws. An unparseable URL, or a cleartext URL in a release build, surfaces through onError with code loadFailed.
iOS PortalConfig.init throws PortalConfigError.invalidBaseURL(URL) when there is no usable scheme or host, and PortalConfigError.insecureBaseURL(URL) for cleartext that is neither loopback nor a honoured dev hatch. Both are LocalizedError, so errorDescription is printable.
Expo The native side builds the same PortalConfig; a config error rejects the presentation and reaches you through onError as loadFailed.
Android The PortalConfig constructor throws IllegalArgumentException for a missing scheme, a missing host, disallowed cleartext, fontScale that is not greater than zero, or a baseUrl carrying a query or fragment. Android is the only platform that rejects a query or fragment this early.

The loopback hosts accepted over plain HTTP differ slightly by platform: iOS allows localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, [::1] and any *.localhost host; Android allows localhost, 127.0.0.1, 10.0.2.2 (the emulator's route to your machine) and ::1; React Native allows localhost, 127.0.0.1 and 10.0.2.2.

locale, theme, fontScale — what the portal is told

These three are the only appearance values that cross the bridge. They are sent during the handshake and can be re-sent at any time without reloading the form — see changing configuration at runtime.

OptionTypeDefaultWhat it changes
locale JS 'en' | 'ar'
Swift PortalLocale.en / .ar
Kotlin PortalLocale.EN / .AR		 React Native sends nothing when you omit it; the native hosts default to en. Selects the portal's translations. ar additionally flips the document direction to RTL, so there is no separate direction flag to set.
theme 'light' | 'dark' | 'system', and the matching Swift and Kotlin enums system Sets the portal's light/dark mode, and also drives the SDK's own overlays. React Native resolves system against the device colour scheme, so the splash matches the form it is covering.
fontScale Number — Swift Double, Kotlin Float 1.0, the portal's own default size The portal maps it to a root font-size adjustment. It must be greater than zero; Android rejects anything else with IllegalArgumentException, both in the constructor and in updateConfigure.

The locale set is closed: en and ar. There is no mechanism for passing a third language through the SDK — portal translations are a portal-side concern, and a value outside that pair is not part of the protocol.

brandColor — your colour on the SDK's own screens

TypeReact Native string (hex) · iOS UIColor? · Android @ColorInt Int? · not available on the Expo sheet
DefaultUnset. The SDK draws with the surface's own foreground colour instead — deliberately plain, rather than substituting some other company's brand.
ScopeThe SDK's loading and retry interstitials only. Never the portal's UI.

brandColor exists because of a timing fact: the loading screen is on the user's display before the WebView can speak, so nothing the portal sends could colour the first frame. It is the one piece of appearance that has to be configured natively instead of arriving over the bridge.

Accepted values

React Native accepts three hex forms only — #rgb, #rrggbb and #rrggbbaa. Anything else is ignored and the default foreground is used instead. That is deliberate: on Android an unparseable colour string throws deep inside the platform's colour processing rather than at the call site, and crashing a host app over a typo in a brand colour is not an acceptable trade. The cost is that a bad value fails quietly, so check that your colour actually renders. 

brandColor: '#121E4C'        accepted
brandColor: '#12E'           accepted
brandColor: '#121E4CCC'      accepted (with alpha)
brandColor: 'navy'           ignored
brandColor: 'rgb(18,30,76)'  ignored

What it tints, exactly

PlatformTintedNot tinted
React NativeThe splash accent and the retry buttonThe portal's own UI
iOSThe loading spinnerThe retry button, which is a stock filled system button
AndroidThe loading progress indicator's tintThe retry button
Expo sheetNothing — the option does not exist—

minPortalVersion — refuse a portal that is too old

TypeString, for example "1.8.0"
DefaultUnset — any portal version is accepted
On failureversionIncompatible through your error handler; the session does not load

Before loading the page the SDK fetches /embed/manifest.json and applies three independent gates. The manifest's bridgeProtocolVersion must equal 1 exactly — a newer protocol is as incompatible as an older one. The manifest's portalVersion must be at least your minPortalVersion. And the SDK's own version must be at least the manifest's minSdkVersion, which is how a portal refuses an app that is too old to talk to it. All three surface as the same code.

Set it to the oldest portal build you have actually tested against, and present versionIncompatible in your UI as "please update the app" rather than as a retry — it is the one error the SDK never auto-retries, because retrying cannot change the answer.

allowedOrigins — extra hosts for main-frame navigation

TypeReact Native and Expo string[] · iOS Set<String>? · Android Set<String>
DefaultThe host of baseUrl, and nothing else
When you need itRarely — only when a portal deployment legitimately navigates the main frame to a second host

The origin derived from baseUrl is always allowed; entries here are added to it. Android accepts either a bare host or a full origin and normalises both to a lower-cased host with any port stripped. iOS defaults the set to the base URL's host when you pass nil.

This is a navigation and bridge-traffic allow-list, not a content blocker: a URL outside it is not loaded into a dead end, it is handed to your onOpenExternal handler, or to the system browser if you have none. On React Native, note that the WebView's originWhitelist is deliberately broad and is not the confinement boundary — allowedOrigins plus the embed-subtree check is.

enableLogging — diagnostics, debug builds only

TypeBoolean
Defaultfalse
Honoured inReact Native: only under __DEV__. iOS and Expo: only in DEBUG builds. Android: forwarded to Logcat, so keep it false in release.

With it on, bridge log messages from the portal and WebView console output reach your platform log. The build gate is not advisory: the protocol requires log messages to be dropped in release builds and the SDK enforces that regardless of the flag, so shipping with it set to true produces no output but does leave a reviewer-visible switch in your code. Drive it from your own debug constant instead.

SDK diagnostics never include credentials or download header values. Keep that property in anything you log on top of it — a bearer token on a log line is a bearer token in a crash report.

allowInsecureHttp — the development hatch

TypeBoolean (allowInsecureHTTP on iOS)
Defaultfalse
PurposePermit a plain http:// base URL for a host that is not loopback

You need this in exactly one situation: the portal dev server is bound to a tenant hostname — for example http://portal-dev.example.com:4200/portal — because the backend resolves the tenant from the request host. Loopback hosts already work over plain HTTP without any flag.

The hatch is build-gated everywhere, so a release binary cannot be talked into cleartext by one boolean in the embedding code:

PlatformGateRelease behaviour
React Native__DEV__Rejected with loadFailed and an "Insecure baseUrl rejected" message
iOS#if DEBUGThe flag is dropped, so the config throws PortalConfigError.insecureBaseURL
Expo#if DEBUG in the native moduleForced to false while the config is parsed
AndroidThe app's FLAG_DEBUGGABLEIgnored, with a warning in Logcat, and the load is refused
The flag alone is not enough

The platform still has to permit cleartext. On iOS, add an App Transport Security exception for the dev domain to Info.plist (or ios.infoPlist in an Expo config). On Android, add a scoped network_security_config in the debug source set for that host. Neither belongs in a release configuration.

certificatePinner — Android only

val config = PortalConfig(
    baseUrl = "https://portal.example.com/portal",
    certificatePinner = { leaf -> myPinSet.contains(fingerprintOf(leaf)) },
)
Type((X509Certificate) -> Boolean)?
Defaultnull — no pinning
CoversSDK-initiated HTTPS only: the manifest fetch and downloads
Does not coverThe portal page load itself
Know the coverage gap before you rely on it

The hook is invoked with the server's leaf certificate; return false to abort the connection. The page load, however, goes through the system WebView network stack, which exposes no pinning hook — so this cannot give you full coverage on its own. If you need that, pin at the network edge. There is no equivalent option on React Native, Expo or iOS.

Changing configuration at runtime

locale, theme and fontScale can be re-applied to a live session — a user switching language in your settings screen should not tear their half-filled form down. Everything else (baseUrl, brandColor, minPortalVersion, allowedOrigins, the security flags) is fixed for the life of a session; to change one of those, end the session and start a new one.

PlatformCall
React Nativeref.current?.configure({ locale: 'ar', theme: 'dark', fontScale: 1.2 })
Expo sheetsession.configure({ locale: 'ar' })
iOS (UIKit)controller.updateConfigure(locale: .ar, theme: .dark, fontScale: 1.2) — every argument is optional
iOS (SwiftUI)Nothing to call. AmthalPortalView diffs config.locale, config.theme and config.fontScale across updates and forwards the changes for you.
Androidview.updateConfigure(...) or fragment.updateConfigure(...)
Two Android constraints

PortalFormActivity exposes updateAuth but no updateConfigure — if you need to re-theme a live session, host the form with PortalFormFragment or AmthalPortalView. And AmthalPortalView.start(...) may be called once per view instance; a second call fails an internal state check, so create a new view for a new session.

Credentials follow the same pattern through a separate call — updateAuth on every platform, or the refresh function handed to React Native's onAuthExpired. The API reference covers auth in full; the configuration-adjacent fact is that credentials travel over the bridge only, never in a URL, which is why there is no token field in any config object on this page.

Theming and branding

What the SDK does not control

The SDK does not theme the portal. A form's colours, logo, typography and layout come from the Client Portal itself, which is themed server-side per branch. No SDK option repaints a form, and none is planned: a host app that could restyle the portal could make one tenant's forms look like another's. What you configure here is the SDK's own screens, plus the three appearance values the portal accepts — locale, theme and fontScale.

Who owns each visible surface
SurfaceOwned byYou change it with
Loading splashSDKbrandColor, or renderLoading on React Native
Error and retry interstitialSDKrenderError on React Native; brandColor partially elsewhere
Session-expired overlaySDKNot configurable — it clears when you supply a fresh token
Sheet chrome (Expo and iOS)SDK and platformPortalSheetOptions — detents, grabber, corner radius
The form itselfPortal, server-side per branchBranch branding in the back office — not the SDK
Form language and directionPortallocale
Form light/dark and text sizePortaltheme, fontScale

Replacing the loading screen on React Native

renderLoading takes the wait over completely. Rather than rebuilding one, reuse the SDK's own splash — it is a public export — and give it your logo: 

import { AmthalPortalForm, PortalSplash } from '@amthal-group/portal-react-native';
import { Image, useColorScheme } from 'react-native';

const dark = useColorScheme() === 'dark';

<AmthalPortalForm
  config={{ baseUrl: 'https://portal.example.com/portal', brandColor: '#121E4C' }}
  renderLoading={() => (
    <PortalSplash
      brandColor="#121E4C"
      dark={dark}
      title="Tasleeh"
      logo={<Image source={require('./assets/logo.png')} style={{ width: 120, height: 40 }} />}
    />
  )}
  /* …the rest of the props… */
/>
PortalSplashProps
PropTypeDefaultNotes
brandColorColorValueUnsetOmit it for a deliberately plain, unbranded wait.
logoReact.ReactNodeUnsetYour own logo, already laid out. Passing one replaces the animated beacon — the two are exclusive on purpose, because a logo and an animated mark on the same screen compete.
darkbooleanfalseThe resolved theme. Turn 'system' into a real value yourself, for example with useColorScheme().
titlestringUnsetShown under the mark; usually the tenant's company name.
captionstringThe SDK's own captionThe default caption changes after eight seconds to acknowledge a slow wait. Supplying your own replaces both.

The SDK never fetches or guesses a logo. A host app has its logo as a local asset, while the portal's is a server-side value whose fallback is Amthal's own mark — the wrong mark to show inside someone else's app. Pass yours, or accept the unbranded default.

The splash also honours the device's reduce-motion setting and drops its animation for users who have asked for that. If you replace it with a screen of your own, keep that behaviour.

Expo sheet presentation options

The Expo wrapper presents the portal in a native iOS sheet, configured separately from PortalSdkConfig through PortalSheetOptions.

OptionTypeDefaultEffect
detentsArray<'large' | 'medium'>['large'] when absent or emptyThe heights the sheet may rest at. When both are offered, it opens at large.
grabberbooleantrueShows the grab handle at the top of the sheet.
cornerRadiusnumberPlatform defaultCorner radius of the sheet card.

Two behaviours are fixed and not configurable: the sheet is presented as a page sheet, and scrolling to the edge of the content does not expand it to the next detent — a form that grows as the user types should not resize the sheet under their finger.

The Expo module is Apple-only, and both wrapper paths contain native code, so neither can run in Expo Go — use a development build. Form delegation is also unsupported on this path: supplying an onFormOp handler makes presentPortalSheet fail fast through onError rather than silently letting the portal call its own endpoints with the wrong identity. Use the inline React Native component for delegated forms.

Before you ship

  1. Base URL carries the deploy path

    Confirm with curl -sI {baseUrl}/embed/manifest.json against the production portal, not only against staging — the two are deployed independently.

  2. No development hatches in the release configuration

    Remove allowInsecureHttp / allowInsecureHTTP, the ATS exception and the Android cleartext config. They are inert at runtime, but they are a review finding.

  3. enableLogging comes from your debug constant

    Never a hardcoded true, and never anything of your own that logs a token.

  4. minPortalVersion is set

    To the oldest portal you have tested, with your UI presenting versionIncompatible as "please update the app" instead of offering a retry that cannot succeed.

  5. brandColor is a value the SDK accepts

    #rgb, #rrggbb or #rrggbbaa. Look at the splash once: an invalid value is ignored rather than reported.

  6. Both locales open cleanly

    Launch a form with locale: 'ar' at least once and confirm the layout mirrors — RTL is where a host app's own surrounding chrome usually breaks first.

Next: the API reference for the component, handle and listener surfaces, or Troubleshooting for what each error code means and which configuration mistake produces it.
